intro_01.text: Hello, and welcome to the Living City. I'm Dr. Celia Mendel, and everything around you is happening inside a single animal cell.
intro_01.speaker: celia

intro_02.text: A small confession: we've slowed everything down and shown only part of it. Real cells are far faster, and far more crowded.
intro_02.speaker: celia

intro_03.text: There's no right order here. Wander, poke at things, and follow whatever catches your eye.
intro_03.speaker: celia

intro_04.text: And whenever you want me, just press G. I'm always happy to talk shop.
intro_04.speaker: celia

tut_move.text: To walk, use W, A, S and D, or simply click the ground. Hold Shift if you're in a hurry.
tut_move.speaker: celia

tut_rotate.text: Press Q or E, or drag with the right mouse button, to turn the view.
tut_rotate.speaker: celia

tut_zoom.text: Scroll to zoom. Scroll all the way out and you'll see the whole city at once.
tut_zoom.speaker: celia

tut_interact.text: See something glowing? Press E, or click it, for a closer look.
tut_interact.speaker: celia

tut_guide.text: Press G whenever you'd like to know what a place is, or where to go next.
tut_guide.speaker: celia

tut_notebook.text: Your field notebook keeps track of everything you find. Press N to open it, and H for the controls.
tut_notebook.speaker: celia

nucleus_arrive.text: This is the nucleus, the control centre. The DNA lives here, and its instructions go out as RNA copies of genes.
nucleus_arrive.speaker: celia

nucleus_more.text: See the pores in that double envelope? There are a few thousand of them. Small molecules slip through; big ones need the right molecular passport.
nucleus_more.speaker: celia

nucleus_try.text: Would you like to try transcribing a gene? Pick one at the console, and we'll walk the messenger RNA out together.
nucleus_try.speaker: celia

nucleus_done.text: Beautifully done. The DNA never leaves; only its RNA copy goes out through the pores to the ribosomes.
nucleus_done.speaker: celia

nucleolus_arrive.text: That glowing orb is the nucleolus. Ribosomal RNA is made here, and the pieces of new ribosomes are put together.
nucleolus_arrive.speaker: celia

nucleolus_more.text: Funny thing: it has no membrane at all. It's more like a droplet that condenses around the ribosomal RNA genes.
nucleolus_more.speaker: celia

nucleolus_try.text: Would you like to try building a ribosome? We'll assemble a small and a large subunit and send them on their way.
nucleolus_try.speaker: celia

nucleolus_done.text: Lovely. The two subunits leave separately, and only clasp together on a messenger RNA out in the cytoplasm.
nucleolus_done.speaker: celia

ribosomes_arrive.text: These little red studs are ribosomes, the protein factories. Each one reads messenger RNA and strings amino acids together.
ribosomes_arrive.speaker: celia

ribosomes_more.text: My favourite part: the actual bond-making is done by RNA, not protein. At heart, the ribosome is an ancient ribozyme.
ribosomes_more.speaker: celia

ribosomes_try.text: Would you like to try translating? Match each codon to its amino acid and watch your protein grow.
ribosomes_try.speaker: celia

ribosomes_done.text: Perfect. Three letters per codon, one amino acid each, until a stop codon says the protein is finished.
ribosomes_done.speaker: celia

rer_arrive.text: These blue corridors are the rough ER. The studs are ribosomes, feeding new proteins straight into the space inside.
rer_arrive.speaker: celia

rer_more.text: A short signal at the start of a protein works like a ticket. It brings the ribosome here and threads the chain through a channel called Sec sixty-one.
rer_more.speaker: celia

rer_try.text: Would you like to try running the production line? Start translation and follow your protein inside.
rer_try.speaker: celia

rer_done.text: Nicely done. Signal, docking, threading, folding: that's how secreted and membrane proteins begin their lives.
rer_done.speaker: celia

ser_arrive.text: Welcome to the smooth ER. No ribosomes here; these tubules make lipids, help detoxify drugs, and store calcium.
ser_arrive.speaker: celia

ser_more.text: In liver cells, enzymes called P four-fifties add oxygen to fat-soluble toxins, making them easier for the body to flush away.
ser_more.speaker: celia

ser_try.text: Would you like to try a detox shift? Catch the drifting toxins and let the enzymes do their work.
ser_try.speaker: celia

ser_done.text: Excellent shift. Smooth ER builds lipids and makes toxins easier to excrete. Your liver is doing exactly this right now.
ser_done.speaker: celia

vesicles_arrive.text: These purple bubbles are transport vesicles: little membrane parcels carrying cargo between compartments and out to the surface.
vesicles_arrive.speaker: celia

vesicles_more.text: They don't really roll on roads. Motor proteins carry them along microtubules: kinesin heads outward, dynein heads back toward the centre.
vesicles_more.speaker: celia

vesicles_try.text: Would you like to launch one? Bud a vesicle from the Golgi and follow it all the way to the membrane.
vesicles_try.speaker: celia

vesicles_done.text: And there's the release. That's exocytosis: the vesicle merges with the cell membrane and its cargo spills outside.
vesicles_done.speaker: celia

golgi_arrive.text: This pink stack is the Golgi apparatus, the shipping centre. Proteins from the ER are finished, sorted and addressed here.
golgi_arrive.speaker: celia

golgi_more.text: Cargo enters at the cis face, nearest the ER, and leaves from the trans face, collecting sugar modifications along the way.
golgi_more.speaker: celia

golgi_try.text: Would you like to try sorting cargo? Tag each parcel with its destination, and the conveyors will do the rest.
golgi_try.speaker: celia

golgi_done.text: Well sorted. Molecular tags, like mannose six-phosphate on lysosomal enzymes, decide where each parcel goes.
golgi_done.speaker: celia

mitochondria_arrive.text: These orange plants are mitochondria, where most of the cell's ATP is made. Listen to those turbines.
mitochondria_arrive.speaker: celia

mitochondria_more.text: The folds inside are cristae, lined with proton pumps. Mitochondria even keep their own little ring of DNA, a souvenir of their bacterial ancestors.
mitochondria_more.speaker: celia

mitochondria_try.text: Would you like to try making some power? Pump protons uphill, then let them spin the turbine.
mitochondria_try.speaker: celia

mitochondria_done.text: Look at it go! Protons flowing back turn ATP synthase, and every full turn makes three ATP.
mitochondria_done.speaker: celia

lysosomes_arrive.text: These green tanks are lysosomes, the recycling plants. Inside, acid-loving enzymes break worn-out parts back into building blocks.
lysosomes_arrive.speaker: celia

lysosomes_more.text: They hold their insides at about pH four and a half to five. The enzymes barely work at neutral pH, which makes a rather clever safety catch.
lysosomes_more.speaker: celia

lysosomes_try.text: Would you like to try some recycling? Feed in a few worn-out parts and watch what happens.
lysosomes_try.speaker: celia

lysosomes_done.text: All digested. Proteins become amino acids, and the cell happily puts every one of them back to work.
lysosomes_done.speaker: celia

vacuoles_arrive.text: These are the storage tanks: vacuoles, holding water, nutrients and a bit of waste.
vacuoles_arrive.speaker: celia

vacuoles_more.text: I'll be honest, the poster flatters them. Animal cell vacuoles are small and varied; it's plant cells that have one enormous central vacuole.
vacuoles_more.speaker: celia

vacuoles_try.text: Would you like to try balancing the tanks? Fill and drain them, and keep the city comfortable.
vacuoles_try.speaker: celia

vacuoles_done.text: Nicely balanced. Animal cells manage water mostly with ion pumps; plants lean on that great central vacuole to stay firm.
vacuoles_done.speaker: celia

membrane_arrive.text: This is the cell membrane, the city boundary. It's a lipid bilayer that decides what comes in and what goes out.
membrane_arrive.speaker: celia

membrane_more.text: In reality it's only about five nanometres thick: a fluid film with proteins drifting through it, not a stone wall.
membrane_more.speaker: celia

membrane_try.text: Would you like to try being the gatekeeper? Decide how each molecule should get across.
membrane_try.speaker: celia

membrane_done.text: Spot on. Oxygen just diffuses, glucose needs a carrier, and the sodium-potassium pump pays for every crossing in ATP.
membrane_done.speaker: celia

cur_nuclear_pore.text: A nuclear pore, up close! Each one handles around a thousand crossings a second, and it's remarkably picky about who gets through.
cur_nuclear_pore.speaker: celia

cur_chromatin_archive.text: The chromatin archive. Two metres of DNA wound onto histone spools. The real trick is knowing which shelves to open.
cur_chromatin_archive.speaker: celia

cur_centrosome.text: Oh, you found the centrosome! It organises the cell's microtubules, and before division it copies itself to form the two spindle poles.
cur_centrosome.speaker: celia

cur_rrna_genes.text: Hundreds of copies of the same gene! Ribosomal RNA is never translated, so the only way to make loads of it is lots of genes.
cur_rrna_genes.speaker: celia

cur_food_truck.text: A free ribosome! Same machine as the ones on the ER, just making proteins for the cytosol, the nucleus or the mitochondria.
cur_food_truck.speaker: celia

cur_signal_ticket.text: There's the ticket: a signal peptide. A short run of water-shy amino acids, and the protein is on its way into the ER.
cur_signal_ticket.speaker: celia

cur_bip_crew.text: Meet BiP, the folding crew. It holds on to sticky, unfolded stretches until the protein gets its shape right.
cur_bip_crew.speaker: celia

cur_calcium_reservoir.text: The calcium reservoir. Open that valve and calcium floods out: muscles contract, hormones are released. Small ion, big consequences.
cur_calcium_reservoir.speaker: celia

cur_grapefruit.text: A grapefruit warning! Grapefruit compounds jam one of the P four-fifty enzymes, so some medicines build up in the blood. Breakfast, it turns out, is pharmacology.
cur_grapefruit.speaker: celia

cur_kinesin_walker.text: Look, a kinesin, walking hand over hand. Eight nanometres a step, one ATP each time.
cur_kinesin_walker.speaker: celia

cur_endocytosis_gate.text: Endocytosis in action! A clathrin cage pulls in a patch of membrane, and the cell swallows whatever was waiting outside.
cur_endocytosis_gate.speaker: celia

cur_cytoskeleton_cables.text: The cytoskeleton. Those cables are scaffolding, tension wires and railway, all at once.
cur_cytoskeleton_cables.speaker: celia

cur_m6p_tag.text: That's the mannose six-phosphate tag, the lysosome's postcode. Without it, digestive enzymes get shipped out of the cell by mistake.
cur_m6p_tag.speaker: celia

cur_cis_trans_signs.text: Cis and trans signs! Cis faces the ER, trans faces the cell surface. Even the Golgi needs to know which way is up.
cur_cis_trans_signs.speaker: celia

cur_mtdna_ring.text: The mitochondrial DNA ring: thirty-seven genes, inherited almost entirely from your mother. Perhaps thank her next time you call.
cur_mtdna_ring.speaker: celia

cur_krebs_roundabout.text: The Krebs roundabout. Carbon comes in, carbon dioxide goes out, and the electrons are handed on to the power plant.
cur_krebs_roundabout.speaker: celia

cur_atp_counter.text: Check that counter. You recycle roughly your own body weight in ATP every single day.
cur_atp_counter.speaker: celia

cur_autophagy.text: Autophagy, literally self-eating. Less grim than it sounds: it's how cells clean house and get through lean times.
cur_autophagy.speaker: celia

cur_ph_gauge.text: pH four and a half. Acidic enough to digest almost anything, and kept that way by proton pumps working nonstop.
cur_ph_gauge.speaker: celia

cur_rubber_duck.text: Is that a rubber duck? That is not an organelle. I'll be having a word with the vacuole crew.
cur_rubber_duck.speaker: celia

cur_aquaporin.text: An aquaporin! Water marches through in single file, billions of molecules a second, while protons are kept firmly out.
cur_aquaporin.speaker: celia

cur_receptor_antenna.text: A receptor antenna. Its family picks up hormones, scents and even light, and about a third of all medicines target it.
cur_receptor_antenna.speaker: celia

cur_peroxisome.text: A peroxisome, our little guest! It breaks down very long fatty acids, and its catalase makes short work of hydrogen peroxide.
cur_peroxisome.speaker: celia

cur_apoptosis_switch.text: Please don't press that! It's apoptosis, a tidy, programmed self-destruct. Your body uses it billions of times a day, just not here, please.
cur_apoptosis_switch.speaker: celia

suggest_nucleus.text: If you haven't been yet, the violet dome is worth a visit. That's the nucleus, and the screens inside are rather mesmerising.
suggest_nucleus.speaker: celia

suggest_rer.text: Those blue terraced rings around the dome are the rough ER. Walk along them and you'll catch proteins being made.
suggest_rer.speaker: celia

suggest_ser.text: Have you found the green ribbon folds yet? That's the smooth ER, quietly making lipids and cleaning up toxins.
suggest_ser.speaker: celia

suggest_golgi.text: The pink stacked building near the front gate is the Golgi. It's the busiest shipping hall in town.
suggest_golgi.speaker: celia

suggest_mitochondria.text: Hear that humming? Follow it to the big orange capsules. Those are the mitochondria, our power plants.
suggest_mitochondria.speaker: celia

suggest_lysosomes.text: Look for the green tanks with the recycling symbol. That's where the lysosomes take old parts apart.
suggest_lysosomes.speaker: celia

suggest_vacuoles.text: The round tanks of turquoise water are the vacuoles. Go and have a look, and keep an eye on the water.
suggest_vacuoles.speaker: celia

suggest_membrane.text: Try walking out to the edge of the city. The membrane gates have far more going on than you'd think.
suggest_membrane.speaker: celia

idle_01.text: Somewhere in your body, all of this is happening right now, in trillions of cells at once. Rather humbling, isn't it?
idle_01.speaker: celia

idle_02.text: I never tire of this place. Every corner is quietly doing something useful.
idle_02.speaker: celia

idle_03.text: You have roughly thirty trillion cells. Most of them are red blood cells, which have thrown out their nucleus entirely.
idle_03.speaker: celia

idle_04.text: Take your time. Science is mostly patient looking, with the occasional gasp.
idle_04.speaker: celia

idle_05.text: If you're wondering where to go next, press G and I'll point you somewhere interesting.
idle_05.speaker: celia

idle_06.text: Listen for a moment. That hum is thousands of machines, each doing one small job very well.
idle_06.speaker: celia

bark_nucleolus_01.text: Ribosome subunits, fresh from the nucleolus! Small ones this way, large ones that way!
bark_nucleolus_01.speaker: worker3

bark_nucleus_01.text: Messenger RNA coming through! Capped, spliced and tailed. Mind the pore!
bark_nucleus_01.speaker: worker3

bark_rer_01.text: No ticket, no entry! Signal sequence first, then into the translocon.
bark_rer_01.speaker: worker3

bark_rer_02.text: Folding crew, we've got a stubborn one here. Send BiP over!
bark_rer_02.speaker: worker3

bark_ser_01.text: Another batch of toxins for the P four-fifties. The liver shift never ends.
bark_ser_01.speaker: worker4

bark_golgi_01.text: Parcel coming through! Glycosylated, labelled and ready to ship!
bark_golgi_01.speaker: worker1

bark_golgi_02.text: Mannose six-phosphate on this one. Lysosome delivery, express!
bark_golgi_02.speaker: worker1

bark_vesicles_01.text: Vesicle departing for the membrane! Kinesin's driving, so hold on tight!
bark_vesicles_01.speaker: worker1

bark_mitochondria_01.text: Mind the turbines. This plant makes the ATP that keeps the whole city running.
bark_mitochondria_01.speaker: worker2

bark_mitochondria_02.text: Keep the oxygen coming! No oxygen at the end of the line, no power for anyone.
bark_mitochondria_02.speaker: worker2

bark_membrane_01.text: Three sodium out, two potassium in. One ATP. Next!
bark_membrane_01.speaker: worker2

bark_lysosomes_01.text: Old parts in, building blocks out. Nothing goes to waste around here.
bark_lysosomes_01.speaker: worker4

bark_lysosomes_02.text: Keep it acidic, team. pH four and a half to five, and not a drop higher.
bark_lysosomes_02.speaker: worker4

bark_vacuoles_01.text: Tanks are topped up. Has anyone seen my duck?
bark_vacuoles_01.speaker: worker4

end_01.text: That's everything: every district, every experiment, every hidden corner. You've seen a whole cell at work. Bravo!
end_01.speaker: celia

end_02.text: The city never stops, of course. Do keep wandering; there's always something new to notice.
end_02.speaker: celia
